erText: Question 3 focussed on discourses about language change and ‘snowflakery’. Students were expected to explore the two texts systematically by describing linguistic features (AO1) and analysing how they created meanings (AO3) in order to evaluate the ways, the texts represented ideas about changing uses of the full stop, showing connections between the texts as parts of wider discourses about language change and woke snowflakery (AO4). Both Text A and B provided students across the ability range with accessible material that enabled them to demonstrate their skills in exploring how discourses work. AO1 The large majority of students understood that they were expected to describe the linguistic features in the texts which they were analysing. Some students still only got marks of 3 or 4 for AO1 and did not seem to recognise the need to describe language features as part of their method of analysis. Generally, the features described were salient and significant for the construction of representations. In some responses linguistic features were identified every time a quotation was made but with little sense of how this feature was significant to the way representations and meanings were being created. Far fewer answers demonstrated the language feature-led technique which hinders Level 4 achievement on AO3 or AO4. Precise linguistic terminology was often in evidence with lots of references to verb types, with useful comments on mental and material processes (though there was frequent uncertainty in the application of these terms). Modal verbs were frequently identified and well analysed. There was good exemplification of sentence and phrase types and the identification of the precise extent of a clause was improved. Issues with pronoun person were less frequent than formerly. Students who looked at sentence and clause features were credited in Level 5 on AO1. These were, however, often the least salient descriptions in an answer. Very few students used these descriptions to analyse the effects the writers were achieving by their deployment of sentence and clause choices. Some things students could profitably address are: • identifying and showing the exact extent of a verb phrase • what counts as post-modification in phrase analysis • what counts as a predicate • distinguishing subordinating and co-ordinating conjunctions from co-ordinate and subordinate clauses • clarifying what the word ‘discourse’ means in the context of this question. AO3 and AO4 Students were generally clear about the purpose of the task and there were few general textual analyses. Almost all recognised the need to compare how the texts were part of discourses about language change, tradition, ‘correct’ English and ‘snowflakery’. There were lots of strong responses which recognised that AO4 is at the heart of this task about discourses by looking at the repetition of ideas across texts and their construction of social identities and reader positions. The most successful answers addressed all the AOs in an integrated way. Most did this throughout their answer, though less successful students confined their comparison to a paragraph at the end or wrote separate paragraphs about similar aspects text by text. Almost all compared the shared focus on changing uses of language, and the full stop in particular. Many reached Level 3 on AO4 because they compared the use of sentence functions, pronouns, the language of the headlines, the use of the term ‘snowflake’ and other features of language. The answers placed in Level 4 could link language with ideas about language change. Often students recognised prescriptivist discourses and made use of Aitchison’s terms to characterise them. They also recognised discourses about snowflakery and being woke. There was a clear improvement in the engagement with the ideas in the texts this year. Most students wrote effectively about how full stops and their use were presented as well as the ways in which young people were satirised and mocked. This enabled a more effective analysis of how the producers of the text created self- representations which affected how the text’s ideas were received by a reader. There was also a lot of work on how the texts positioned a potential reader and used language to shape their views. Modality was frequently looked at. Some students had difficulties disentangling the different views within the texts. The best answers had a clear understanding of how Bancroft positioned the views of Doctor Lauren Fonteyn and Professor Celia Clin and how Weaver presented the university research. Some students had difficulty disentangling the audiences of the texts from the imagined or ironic addressees within the texts. More successful answers: • placed the texts, and ideas within them, within prescriptivist and descriptivist discourses • analysed discourses of correctness, tradition, decay, snowflakery • identified and compared the views of Sheridan in Text A the presentation of the research findings by Bancroft in Text B • contrasted the views and ideas of Klin and Fonteyn with the views of the authors • contrasted the language of Klin and Fonteyn with that of the authors • compared and evaluated how Text B’s use of quotations gave the views more weight than the brief reference to Fonteyn’s ‘comments’ in A • considered how ‘according to experts’ and ‘academic paper’ might have negative connotations (in contrast to common sense and tradition) rather than being an endorsement and compared them with Sheridan’s passive ‘They are said to….’ • compared how both articles sensationalised the story: ‘under the spotlight again’ and ‘Feverish debate broke out last week….’ and evaluated the hyperbolic attempts to provoke disbelief and anger • compared the way both articles represented and judged the young’s views of the full stop as aggressive, abrupt, blunt, angry • compared the representation of the full stop as harmless, humble, innocent • compared the representation of the full stop as traditional, long-standing, useful, creating clarity • compared ways the texts infantilised younger people and treated them as immature with the intertextuality of ‘big bad full stop’ and the metaphor of being ‘weaned on text messages’ • compared the representation of the young as sensitive, easily intimidated, overly anxious • compared the positioning of the reader in the headlines • analysed the disbelieving tone of the thematised adverbial ‘Now’ and the capitalised ‘FULL STOPS’ in Text B’s headline and how these represented snowflakery and compared Sheridan’s use of ellipsis in her first paragraph to show her disbelief • compared how Text A assumed the position and voice of a young person or addressed them directly to satirise them with the use of address in the first sentence of Bancroft’s article • explored how both texts created a generational divide by the use of pronouns, the identification of a ‘generation’ and references to ‘youngsters’ and ‘Older people’ • explored how Text A created a nightmare vision of a totalitarian woke world run by woke chief constables and the Keypad Cops • evaluated Sheridan’s use of hyperbole, alliteration, punning, neologism, sentence shaping and punctuation use to make her points playfully yet powerfully • analysed Sheridan’s address to her imagined sympathetic reader at the end to position them and their response • analysed Sheridan’s self-presentation as put-upon traditionalist accused of being a stuffy stick-in-the-mud and compared Bancroft’s appeals to tradition and the length of time full stops have been used • considered how the reference to Aristophanes made the audience perceive the full-stop • noted the conventions regarding full stops in the headline and sub-editorial from the MailOnline. erText: Students were asked to a write an opinion article in which they assessed the ideas presented in the texts they had analysed in question 3. These texts raised issues about changing uses of punctuation, linguistic conventions and etiquette. Students were expected to show knowledge and understanding of linguistic concepts and issues (AO2) when writing in a journalistic style for a non-specialist audience (AO5). This task asked students to take their knowledge of English Language and engage with, and intervene in, real- world debates. Again, this year this question was often answered less effectively than the other questions on the paper. Students generally understood the AO5 requirements of the task and most had clear ideas about the demands of writing feature or opinion pieces. The mean mark for AO2, however, was significantly below the mean marks for AO2 in Section A. Many struggled to select and deploy knowledge effectively. This was sometimes caused by a rather imprecise focus on the actual issues raised in the texts. A major distinguishing factor therefore was the recognition of the need to provide a satisfying level of information and argument about the linguistic issues. Nonetheless, many students recognised the need to integrate explicit linguistic knowledge into a text for a non-specialist audience. Some of the most effective responses began by explaining to their readers the views and arguments of Sheridan and those reported in Text B before dismantling them. More successful responses focussed on identifying and classifying the attitudes to language expressed in the sources. Most focussed on the issues of language change and relatively few the issues about young people being woke snowflakes. Less successful responses wrote rather broadly about language change as natural and found it difficult to find a clear focus for their article and develop an argument. Almost all students this year were prepared to write an article and provided a functional headline. Many also provided engaging sub-editorial features and arresting openings, though there were fewer really clinching conclusions as time ran out for many. Many recognised the need to link their article to having read the articles in question 3. This was done more effectively than in previous series with fewer elaborately contrived scenarios and late- night doom-scrolling. Far fewer responses referred to ‘Text A’ or ‘Text B’. There were still a few essay-like and over-academic answers, but far more very informal responses which did not inform in a satisfying way. There were a number of responses that relied on abuse of Weaver Sheridan and Holly Bancroft, boomers or the old in general. More successful answers: • focussed very tightly on the issues of changing uses of punctuation or etiquette in phone or online communication • cited the ideas of Sheridan and Bancroft so that they could challenge them • helped the reader to identify the ways of thinking about language they represented • located attitudes to change within discourses of correctness and tradition • classified the prescriptivist outlook, often identifying declinism or sticklerism as key discourses about language change • used Aitchison’s metaphors to categorise explanations of change as decay, laziness or an unwelcome spread or invasion • linked the articles with others that formed the discourse, many quoting John Humphrys • placed the views of young people within anti-woke discourses clustered around ideas of the young as snowflakes • challenged and evaluated the ideas in the sources and offered alternative views • examined other examples of changes, evaluating them from different points of view • examined the nature of texting as a mode of communication, trying to replicate aspects of spoken language • introduced language researchers by first and last name and indicated who they were for an unfamiliar audience • explored ideas of potential, implementation, diffusion and codification to explain how and why changes came about • discussed wave models, s-curves and style to style changes to explore how uses of language are spread • use Deutscher’s principles of economy and expressiveness to offer more neutral explanations • examined the nature of texting as a mode of communication, trying to replicate aspects of spoken language, referring to McWhorter’s idea of ‘fingered speech’ • discussed ways in which being woke affected language use and why • mounted a defence of being sensitive and aware when using language • developed a convincing persona and voice and addressed the experiences of their imagined audience • deployed techniques seen in the sources, shaping their syntax powerfully for effect • played with sentence punctuation, semantic fields and neologism to create engaging texts. Less successful answers: • re-hashed the views of Sheridan and Bancroft and approved the need to maintain correct use of punctuation • did not provide the reader with ideas and information about changing uses of language • wrote generally about language change as inevitable and natural • relied on assertion or abuse as a way of responding to the sources • let their creation of a persona and scenario take over from the conveying of linguistic ideas • wrote in an essay format • introduced names of language researchers without any explanation of who they were • introduced linguistic terms and concepts without any explanation for the non-specialist reader.

erText: Analyse how Text A uses language to create meanings and representations. Text A is an article from Mail Online published in 2020. It is about a campaign in Australia to remove statues of the 18th century explorer Captain James Cook. How students did well Students did well when they: • were able to engage in detail with different representations of Cook, the protestors and people in support of keeping the statue. • explored ideas about power through analysis of the journalist’s descriptions of some of the different people within the text, such as referring to protestors generally, ‘one woman’, in comparison with the more respectful address of authoritative figures such as the Prime Minister. • engaged with specific language details that positioned the audience as rejecting the stance of protesters. • explored how material verbs were used, such as ‘torn down’, ‘two other statues…have already been defaced’, ‘ripping the pages’, suggesting the violence and irrationality of protestors. • explored how this audience positioning was emphasised through punctuation choices, such as enclosing abstract nouns ‘colonialism and genocide’ in inverted commas to cast doubt on the assertions about Cook’s role in these atrocities. • evaluated the journalistic context to consider whether Mail Online was being neutral, presenting bias subtly through their language choices, or if they were responding to the global social contexts of the time (BLM). • offered relevant and perceptive comments about wider cultural and social factors, referencing ideas about colonialism, rights of Indigenous people, British power and rule, as well as recent events such as BLM which may have driven this wave of protests. • supported these points with carefully chosen linguistic description, applying terms accurately and precisely to analyse and evaluate representations in detail. • referred to a wide range of features from the text, including noun phrases, verb choices, a variety of verb tenses and varied sentence and clause types. • were able to comment on how these language choices were used to shape textual meanings, such as the use of passive voice to place emphasis on the destruction of the statue. How students did less well Students did less well when they: • were led by AO1: this meant that they focused heavily on linguistic description, labelling features in detail but not engaging with textual meanings, contexts and representations. • followed the pattern of providing quotations with linguistic labels but with minimal discussion of the effect of these features. • focussed on the contexts of the text, referring to ideas about Captain Cook’s statue and the protestors in some detail, but lacking any linguistic description. • applied inaccurate labels to language features, frequently confusing word classes, for example describing ‘forced’ as a verb without considering its use within the noun phrase ‘forced removal’. • edited quotations from the text to fit their language descriptions. • described features as a ‘pattern’ without recognising patterning of features across the text. • were distracted by their own thoughts about colonialism or BLM, which led to some move away from analysis of language detail and features which created these ideas and representations within the text.

erText: Analyse how Text B uses language to create meanings and representations. Text B is an extract from a book titled The History of Cleveland, written by Reverend John Graves in 1808. In a section of the village of Marton, Yorkshire, Graves writes about the achievements of Captain James Cook, who was born there. How students did well Students did well when they: • commented on the positive descriptions of Captain Cook within the text. • offered detailed and thoughtful analyses. • engaged with the genre of the text as a history book and a local history focussed on Yorkshire. • responded in detail to the varied representations of Cook within the text, discussing his achievements, legacy, personal ambitions and determination, linked to specific linguistic detail • explored the writer’s reverence for Cook as almost God-like. • placed this within the local and regional context. • considered the significance of religion at the time of publication, evaluating the implications of a Reverend describing Captain Cook in such glorified terms. • explored ideas about patriotic attitudes to Britain’s colonial ambitions that Cook had helped to fulfil. • identified a range of features, including noun phrases, conditional clauses and a variety of modal verb choices. • identified grammatical patterns in the data of repeated complex, multi-clausal sentences. • analysed these not only as typical of the time period but linked them to representations of Cook, such as the use of a syndetic list of verbs and the power of adjectives to represent the writer’s attitudes to Cook. • provided sustained reference to language features in detail to explore textual meanings, contexts and representations. How students did less well Students did less well when they: • offered extensive linguistic description but with little discussion of textual meanings and contexts. • engaged with ideas about Cook and his fame but didn’t offer linguistic details to explore these ideas in detail. • found the older style of the text challenging and found it difficult to move beyond the long s and complexity of sentence types . • attempted to apply linguistic labels with limited accuracy, such as confusing word classes. • over-stated the significance of the pronoun ‘he’ and ‘his’ • confused dynamic and stative verbs. • referred to semantic fields without clear exemplification, sometimes with only one example of a single word, and sometimes with no exemplification at all. • did not engage with the genre of the text as a history book and a local history focused on Yorkshire which led to missed opportunities to consider contextual factors in detail • assumed that Cook was Australian, so missed the fact that this was a text celebrating a local, Yorkshire person of note. • offered their personal thoughts about the ideas expressed within the text and their own response to colonialism and often struggled to move past these to analyse the language use within the text.

erText: Explore the similarities and differences in the ways that Text A and Text B use language. How students did well Students did well when they: • compared language features across the two texts so were able to move into level 3. • linked language with aspects of context and representation. • began their comparisons with a focus on language which proved a useful starting point from which they could then explore wider ideas and representations. • compared language features such as syndetic listing, the role and function of graphological features, proper nouns and noun phrases and verb choices. • developed their focus on language comparisons to discuss how these features linked to wider contextual factors, such as changing attitudes towards Cook and his legacy over time. • evaluated these shifting attitudes in light of the texts themselves, especially in comparison of a history book and an online article. • considered the role of the text producers in shaping the information for their audiences. • reflected on changing attitudes towards colonialism and imperialism. erText: ‘Experimenting with language is essential to a child’s language development.’ Referring to Data Set 1 in detail, and to relevant ideas from language study, evaluate this view of children’s language development. Data Set 1: David (4 years, 8 months) and Seth (1 year, 10 months) are talking in the back of their father’s car. They are on their way home for their evening meal after spending the day with their grandparents. How students did well Students did well when they: • made close reference to a range of features, mainly adjacency pairs, imperatives, types of nouns and prosody. • labelled structural patterns of the interaction, such as the use of imperatives, linking these to David’s role in leading the discussion and resulting in the subsequent pattern of Seth’s use of concrete nouns. • discussion of verb + object patterns, sometimes linked to Brown’s classification of syntactic structures. • referred to examples of simple structures as illustrative of child directed speech strategies. • provided some detailed description of phonological features. • demonstrated secure knowledge of a range of theories and research. • were able to discuss ideas about social interaction and the role of the more knowledgeable other, whether that was David or Dad. • addressed Behaviourist views in some detail, with clear reference to imitation and reinforcement. • referenced Chomsky and discussed ideas about Universal Grammar. • took examples from outside the data, such as reference to Berko-Gleason’s study. • engaged with strategies to shape Seth’s schema. • addressed ideas about cognitive stages of development or object permanence • discussed Seth’s use of ‘indowdoor’ as illustrating affixation and morphological structures. • referred to Tomasello and engaged with ideas about intention-reading and pattern- finding. • engaged with the nature of experimentation, seeing it as a factor of play and evaluating its pragmatic function. How students did less well Students did less well when they: • struggled to engage with the focus on experimentation, showing less certainty with the application of relevant theory. • provided detailed accounts of learned theory, discussing ideas surrounding nature and nurture, thus losing focus on the actual question. • tended to drift from the data set, with minimal focus on the exchange between David, Seth and their father. • attempted to apply innatist views, but not always successfully, such as describing aspects of Seth’s language as featuring virtuous errors. • noted cognitive development but did not discuss it in detail.

What students did well Students did well when they: • explored what ‘improvement’ in language might actually mean • evaluated specific changes as improvements, deteriorations or simply changes • evaluated the metaphor of language evolution • interpreted Crystal’s tides metaphor with examples • considered Deutscher’s ideas of economy and creativity as drivers of change • challenged descriptivist stances • explored random fluctuation theory as a challenge to the idea of improvement • looked at functional explanations of language change to enable communication • examined cultural transmission and sub-stratum explanations of change • examined metaphors of language change as decay, laziness, invasion, infection • evaluated language reform and benign prescriptivism as attempts to improve how language represented society and individuals • evaluated the effectiveness of politically correct or woke language and illustrated Pinker’s Euphemism Treadmill • assessed whether reclamations were improvements • explored and evaluated the creation of pidgins and creoles • evaluated changes caused by English as a colonial or global language • weighed up the advantages and disadvantages of standardisation • evaluated the process of dialect levelling • evaluated the effect of new technologies from the printing press to the mobile phone • assessed the emergence of Multi-cultural London English • assessed borrowings, especially Americanisms • analysed specific examples from different perspectives. against regional accents in the past • explained how regional accents were seen as ‘too common’ and subject to snobbery while RP was seen as posh • compared how Rosseinsky and Deacon presented changes in attitudes over time • examined the idea that regional accents were a source of mockery • identified how some people in the media were seen to be adopting less posh sounding accents to sound more relatable • compared Leith’s hatred of her RP accent with Rajan’s criticism of its unrepresentative presence in the media • noted Deacon’s rejection of Rajan’s criticism about regional accents being under- represented • compared how the writers criticised Leith for complaining about her advantages from RP and Rajan for his inverted snobbery towards RP • compared how the writers presented their critiques of Prue Leith and Amol Rajan, looking at address and naming patterns • analysed how Text B othered and undermined Rajan’s views (In his view, According to Rajan, he believes, he claims) and compared how Text A belittled Leith’s woes (squirming, moaning, cringe) • analysed how Rosseinsky and Deacon presented their own views and arguments, noting how she saw an ongoing issue while he downplayed the issues nowadays • saw how they both treated attitudes to accents as part of wider social values • compared how Rosseinsky showed her annoyance with Leith’s unhappiness about an accent that gave her huge advantages with Deacon’s presentation of Rajan’s ‘inverted snobbery’ • analysed how the self-presentation of the writers and their positioning of the reader worked persuasively • analysed modality in the presentation of ideas and views • compared and evaluated the ways the articles began in their first paragraphs • analysed how Text B’s single simple sentence paragraphs erText: Write an opinion article on attitudes to accents. In your article you should: • assess the ideas and issues raised in Text A and Text B • refer to ideas from language study • argue your own views. How students did well Students did well when they: • had a clear understanding of the op-ed genre • referred to the articles to which they were responding and identified the ideas and issues they raised, drawing on their successful identification in their answer to Question 3 • explained why Prue Leith might hate her RP accent and how it might be a hindrance • explained how regional accents were seen as ‘too common’ • identified how some people in the media were adopting less posh sounding accents to sound more relatable • noted Deacon’s rejection of Rajan’s criticism about regional accents being under- represented • noted Rosseinsky’s view of accents as a barrier to social mobility • referred to and gave further examples of people changing their accents • looked at a range of attitudes to standard and non-standard accents • used various surveys and matched guise experiments to support this discussion • explored the pros and cons of both standard and non-standard accents • explored ideas about repertoires, code-switching and accommodation • established that attitudes to accent were based on social not linguistic grounds • evaluated changing accents as a response to prejudice and discrimination • identified the phenomenon of ‘accentism’ as a form of discrimination • argued that accents need to be treated as a protected characteristic • used witty sub-editorial material that hooked a reader and indicated the line of argument • made the issues concrete and relevant to the shared world of the writer and audience • informed the reader about linguistic concepts and research in an accessible manner • introduced researchers by first and second name to personalise the material and with an explanatory phrase to explain who they were • showed close control of sentence patterns, some of which were picked up from the articles. How students did less well Students did less well when they: • wrote a Section A style essay • did not use 1st and 2nd person pronouns • used an overly informal address to the reader • did not provide any linguistic information to develop a response to the articles • referred to the articles as ‘Text A’ and ‘Text B’ • did not transform linguistic ideas and terms for the reader • referred to linguists by their surname and gave no explanation of who they were or gave them inappropriate epithets • lost focus on accents, often for dialects, elaborated and restricted code, attitudes to language change • wrote long and over-elaborate explanations of how they came across the articles or scenarios • wrote that attitudes to accents ‘weren’t that deep’ and didn’t really matter.
